questions.q: Why does launching a std::thread for each of a thousand small pricing tasks scale poorly?
options: std::thread cannot be constructed more than a hundred times per program
Each thread reserves its own stack and incurs creation/teardown overhead, and the OS must context-switch between far more threads than available cores
std::thread objects cannot run functions that return a value
Only one std::thread can exist at a time per process
questions.explain: Per-thread stack memory, thread creation/teardown cost, and excessive context switching beyond the number of available cores all add overhead that outweighs the actual work for many small tasks.

questions.q: In the ThreadPool example, what does calling submit() do?
options: It creates a brand-new worker thread for that task
It pushes the task onto a shared queue and notifies a worker thread, without creating any new thread
It blocks until the task finishes running
It immediately runs the task on the calling thread
questions.explain: submit() locks the queue, pushes the task, and calls notify_one() to wake an already-existing worker — the fixed set of worker threads is created once, in the pool's constructor, not per task.

questions.q: What does std::future<T>::get() do if the result is not yet ready?
options: It throws an exception immediately
It returns a default-constructed T
It blocks the calling thread until the result becomes available, then returns it
It returns a null pointer
questions.explain: get() blocks until the asynchronous operation completes and the result is available, then returns that result (or rethrows an exception if the task threw one).

questions.q: Why pass std::launch::async explicitly to std::async rather than relying on the default launch policy?
options: Because std::async does not compile without an explicit launch policy
Because without it, the implementation may defer running the task lazily on the thread that calls get(), rather than guaranteeing a separate thread
Because std::launch::async disables the returned future
Because the default policy always runs the task on the main thread only
questions.explain: The default launch policy lets the implementation choose deferred execution, running the task only when get() or wait() is called — possibly on the calling thread, not concurrently. std::launch::async requests genuine concurrent execution.

questions.q: Why does task granularity matter when submitting work to a thread pool?
options: Because the pool rejects tasks below a certain size
Because if each task is too small, the overhead of queuing and dequeuing it exceeds the actual work done, wasting more time than it saves
Because granularity determines how many worker threads are created
Because only tasks returning void can be submitted
questions.explain: A thread pool only pays off when each task's work is large enough to amortize the cost of locking the queue, waking a worker, and dispatching the task. Too-fine-grained tasks spend more time on coordination than computation.
